what_interviewers_test: Whether the candidate can decide what to build and why: frame a goal tied to the company's mission/business, pick a specific user segment, surface real (not generic) pain points, generate distinct solutions, choose one with explicit criteria and trade-offs, and say how success would be measured. Meta (Product Sense) leans on segmentation rigour, mission alignment and a follow-up conflicting-metric/trade-off probe; Google (Product Design / Product Sense, plus 'favourite product') adds bold/visionary thinking, user empathy for non-obvious needs and, in the favourite-product variant, constructive critique versus competitors. Amazon tests it through customer obsession / working backwards rather than a dedicated round; Uber uses a jam session / presentation; Indian consumer-tech companies (Swiggy, Flipkart, Zomato, Meesho) test empathy for Indian (often Bharat/tier-2/3) users and tie design to business outcomes and metrics. [uncertain: India specifics are from prep aggregators and a few candidate reports]
format_variants: Live, candidate-led is the default (Meta Product Sense 45 min with ~35 min core case; Google ~45 min; corpwaters reports 25-30 min of case in a 30-min slot). Interviewer-led variants: interviewer redirects to a segment or asks follow-ups (Meta almost always shifts into a conflicting-metric scenario at the end). Favourite-product variant: candidate picks a product, explains why it works for a specific user, critiques it, and proposes improvements; often 15-20 min inside a longer round. AI-era variant (Meta 'Product Sense with AI', piloted from late 2025; Google/AI-native firms): ~30 min case then ~30 min prototyping with an AI tool; prototype judged on linkage to earlier reasoning, not polish. Take-home (more common at Indian startups and for senior roles [uncertain]): written PRD/deck; expectations shift toward depth of user research, rollout and metrics because time is not constrained. For a transcript-only grader, treat the prototyping portion as out of scope and score only spoken reasoning.

dimensions.name: Goal and product motivation
dimensions.definition: States why the product/improvement matters: the company mission or business objective, the goal of this design (e.g. engagement, acquisition, retention, monetisation), and any constraints/assumptions.
dimensions.signal_sought: Direction is grounded in this company's mission, strategy and advantages, not generic; goal chosen deliberately and used later to prioritise.
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the sentence where the candidate states the goal/mission and any line where they later reuse that goal to choose a segment, problem or solution (e.g. 'Since our goal is repeat orders in tier-2 cities, I'll prioritise...').

dimensions.name: User segmentation and choice
dimensions.definition: Maps the ecosystem/user types, segments them along meaningful (behavioural/motivational/need-based, not just demographic) lines, and picks one target segment with explicit criteria.
dimensions.signal_sought: Non-overlapping segments specific to this product; prioritisation reasoned on more than one criterion (size, pain severity, underserved, strategic fit); optional persona.
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the list of segments, the criteria used, and the sentence choosing the target segment with its justification.

dimensions.name: Pain point identification and prioritisation
dimensions.definition: Walks through the chosen user's journey or context, lists several specific problems (not needs or solutions), and picks the one to solve with stated criteria.
dimensions.signal_sought: Pain points feel discovered from the user's actual day, span different root causes, are separated from solutions, and are prioritised on frequency/severity/goal fit.
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the journey steps or scenario, the enumerated pain points, and the sentence selecting the priority pain point and why.

dimensions.name: Solution breadth and creativity
dimensions.definition: Generates multiple genuinely distinct solutions tied to the chosen pain point, ranging from incremental to bold, and describes at least one concretely enough to picture (v1/MVP experience).
dimensions.signal_sought: Ideas could fail independently; at least one non-obvious or visionary idea; solutions leverage company-specific assets; concrete v1 description.
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote each named solution and the concrete description of the chosen one (what the user sees/does).

dimensions.name: Prioritisation and trade-offs
dimensions.definition: Chooses among solutions with explicit criteria (impact on goal, effort, risk, confidence) and articulates downsides, risks and what is deliberately deferred.
dimensions.signal_sought: Criteria named before the choice; trade-offs acknowledged (cannibalisation, ecosystem side effects on merchants/drivers, cost, complexity); mitigation or 'what would need to be true' for deferred ideas.
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the comparison (e.g. impact/effort reasoning) and any sentence naming a risk, trade-off or mitigation.

dimensions.name: Success metrics
dimensions.definition: Defines how the chosen solution's success would be measured: a primary metric linked to the stated goal, plus guardrail/counter metrics.
dimensions.signal_sought: Primary metric operationally defined and tied to the goal; 1-3 guardrails that capture plausible harm; not a laundry list.
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the named primary metric, its definition, and guardrail metrics with their rationale.

dimensions.name: Structure, communication and collaboration
dimensions.definition: Lays out a game plan, signposts transitions, states assumptions, checks in at key decisions, and handles interviewer redirects/pushback by integrating them.
dimensions.signal_sought: Interviewer always knows where the candidate is and why; candidate drives the case without needing hand-holding; adapts when given new information.
dimensions.transcript_evidence: Quote the opening plan, transition statements, check-in questions, and the response to any interviewer pushback or redirect.

recommended.reasoning: Erez rubric makes it a must-pass dimension but allots only 3-5 of ~35 min; Aced 'business acumen' is 1 of 5 equal dimensions (20%). Recommended 10% because in a transcript most of the business framing is also credited inside segment/solution choices.

Erez gives 8-10 min (~27% of time) to segmentation; Aced folds segmentation and pain points into 'user-centricity' (20%); Meta candidate accounts single out segmentation clarity. Split user-centricity across two dimensions.
Erez 8-10 min (~27%); corpwaters expects 5-7 problems then a reasoned selection; Aced user-centricity. Slightly above segmentation because generic pain points are the most cited failure.
Erez solution development 8-10 min; Aced 'product taste' 20%; Google accounts stress bold ideas. Highest single weight, all sources agree it is core.

IGotAnOffer (ex-Meta coach) rubric has an explicit trade-off criterion; Aced scores deprioritisation inside product taste; Erez embeds it in 'prioritized choice'. Separated here so an 8B grader can find the evidence.

Disagreement: Erez's product sense rubric has no metrics dimension (metrics belong to Meta's Analytical round), while Meta candidate accounts report feedback on metrics depth and corpwaters lists metrics/guardrails as a strong-answer marker. 10% is a compromise; raise to 15% for Indian companies and Google where metrics are reported inside design rounds [uncertain].

Erez 'clear communication' and Aced 'communication & collaboration' are both full dimensions (20% in Aced). Reduced to 13% because the grader should not reward structure alone (see recitation_vs_insight).

source_disagreements: No company publishes numeric weights. Erez (Lenny's, Apr 2025) and Aced (2026) both imply equal-weighted dimensions with a must-pass bar on each ('excellence in one area can't compensate for weakness in another'); IGotAnOffer (Oct 2026) says an exceptional area may sometimes offset a borderline one but minimum bar still applies.
Metrics: Erez rubric excludes them; Meta-reported feedback and corpwaters include them.
Aced adds 'prototyping ability' (AI-era) as a full dimension; excluded here because the grader sees only the transcript. If a prototype narration exists, fold it into Solution breadth.
Corpwaters warns against over-fixating on mission; Aced rewards strong mission/business linkage. Resolution: credit goal framing only when it is used to drive later choices.
weights.alternative_equal_weight_view: If following Erez/Aced literally: 5 dimensions x 20% (communication, motivation/business, segmentation+pain points as user-centricity, solution/taste, plus prototyping or metrics). [uncertain]

must_pass_gates.gate: Jumps to solutions before choosing a target user segment and a specific pain point
No goal or mission stated and no criteria used for any choice (all choices arbitrary)
Only one solution proposed (no breadth) or all ideas are variants of one concept
must_pass_gates.cap: Solution dimension <=2 and overall max Lean Hire

must_pass_gates.gate: Any must-pass dimension (segmentation, pain points, solution, communication) scored 1
must_pass_gates.cap: overall max No Hire regardless of average

must_pass_gates.gate: Never lands: runs out of time without a chosen solution
Solution not connected to the chosen pain point/segment (drift)
must_pass_gates.source: https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/the-definitive-guide-to-mastering (listing features without tying to pain points)

must_pass_gates.gate: Answers with 'I would first do user research' instead of generating own ideas

Goal and product motivation.1: No goal or mission; starts listing features. ('So I'd add a dark mode and a chatbot.')
Goal and product motivation.2: Generic or checkbox mission not used later. ('Swiggy's mission is to deliver food, so the goal is engagement.')
Goal and product motivation.3: Company-specific goal with reason, stated assumptions, and reused to make a later choice. ('Instamart growth is the priority, so I'll optimise for second-week repeat orders.')
Goal and product motivation.4: Explains why this company, with its assets and timing, should build this now; goal visibly drives every downstream choice. ('PhonePe already owns the UPI moment at the counter, so the leverage is...')

User segmentation and choice.2: Demographic-only or overlapping segments; picks largest without criteria. ('Students, working professionals, elderly. I'll pick students.')
User segmentation and choice.3: Need/behaviour-based, non-overlapping segments incl. ecosystem sides; picks one using 2+ named criteria.
User segmentation and choice.4: Segments that could only belong to this product; choice argued on pain, size, underservedness and strategic fit; considers other ecosystem sides (merchants, riders, sellers). ('First-time Meesho resellers in tier-3 who sell via WhatsApp...')

Pain point identification and prioritisa.1: No pain points, or lists solutions disguised as problems.
Pain point identification and prioritisa.2: 1-2 generic pain points that fit any product; no prioritisation.
Pain point identification and prioritisa.3: 3-5 specific pain points from a journey walk-through, distinct root causes, one prioritised with stated criteria (frequency, severity, goal fit).
Pain point identification and prioritisa.4: Pain points feel discovered (concrete moments in the user's day), separated from solutions, prioritised with a non-obvious but convincing call.

Solution breadth and creativity.1: No solution or a single obvious feature.
Solution breadth and creativity.2: 2-3 ideas that are variations of one concept or generic ('use AI to personalise').
Solution breadth and creativity.3: 3+ distinct ideas grounded in the priority pain point, incl. at least one bold idea; chosen one described concretely (v1 flow).
Solution breadth and creativity.4: At least one surprising idea leveraging company-specific assets; spectrum from MVP to moonshot; v1 described as a user experience with edge cases.

Prioritisation and trade-offs.1: Picks a solution with no reason.
Prioritisation and trade-offs.2: One-dimensional reason ('easiest to build') or a 2x2 with no actual reasoning.
Prioritisation and trade-offs.3: Compares options on impact vs effort/risk tied to the goal; names at least one trade-off or risk.
Prioritisation and trade-offs.4: Multi-dimensional comparison, explicit deprioritisation with 'what would need to be true', second-order/ecosystem effects and mitigations (e.g. impact on delivery partners or seller margins).

Success metrics.1: No metrics, or vanity metric only ('downloads').
Success metrics.2: Lists many metrics without a primary, or primary not tied to goal.
Success metrics.3: One primary metric operationally defined and tied to the goal plus 1-2 guardrails. ('Weekly repeat-order rate among new tier-2 users; guardrail: delivery time and cancellation rate.')
Success metrics.4: Primary + guardrails + counter-metric with rationale and a sketch of how to validate (experiment or leading indicator), anticipates metric conflict.

Structure, communication and collaborati.1: Hard to follow; no plan; needs the interviewer to drive.
Structure, communication and collaborati.2: Followable but reads as a monologue or rigid template; asks interviewer what to do next.
Structure, communication and collaborati.3: Opening game plan, clear transitions, check-ins at key decisions, integrates redirects.
Structure, communication and collaborati.4: Conversational and adaptive throughout; handles pushback/conflicting-metric follow-ups by linking back to earlier reasoning; interviewer feels like a participant.

level_expectations.APM / entry: Solid (3) = clear structure, reasonable segmentation with one criterion beyond size, 3+ specific pain points, 3 distinct solutions, one primary metric. Creativity and business linkage can be lighter; hints tolerated once or twice with small deduction. Erez says rubric is broadly consistent across levels, so the shift is in depth, not dimensions.
level_expectations.PM / mid: Solid = multi-criteria prioritisation at each step, at least one bold idea, guardrail metrics, trade-offs named unprompted, drives case with minimal steering. Corpwaters: cannot advance beyond mid-level by focusing only on features.
level_expectations.Senior PM+: Solid = business-owner lens (strategy, ecosystem, operations, monetisation), company-specific why-now, decisions under ambiguity without asking for validation, second-order effects and rollout risk, crisp handling of conflicting-metric follow-ups. Feature-only answers cap at 2 on Goal and Trade-offs. [level shifts largely interviewer-account/inferred]

green_flags: States goal and a short game plan in the first 2-3 minutes, with explicit assumptions.
Segments by need/behaviour/frequency, includes other ecosystem sides (sellers, riders, restaurants), and justifies the chosen segment with 2+ criteria.
Walks through a concrete user journey and names specific moments of friction; separates problems from solutions.
Offers a spectrum of solutions (safe MVP, aggressive, moonshot) that could each fail independently.
Names criteria before choosing and explicitly says what is deprioritised and why.
Defines one primary metric tied to the goal plus guardrails/counter-metrics.
Checks in at decision points and folds interviewer pushback into the reasoning.
India context: designs for low bandwidth, vernacular, low-trust/COD, UPI flows, or tier-2/3 simplicity when the prompt's users warrant it. [uncertain: prep-platform/practitioner accounts]
red_flags: Recites Goal-User-Problem-Solution template with generic content that would fit any product.
Jumps to features before picking a user and problem.
Demographic-only or overlapping segments; picks the biggest group with no criteria.
Lists needs or solutions as 'pain points'; only 1-2 pain points.
Single solution, or ideas that are variants of one concept; 'add AI/personalisation' with no specifics.
No trade-offs or reasons; prioritises by 'easiest'.
Laundry list of metrics, or none; vanity metrics only.
Seeks validation ('Do we have a solution in mind?', 'What do stakeholders want?') or defers to 'I'd do research first'.
recitation_vs_insight: Recitation: every framework step is present but contents are interchangeable across products (segments like 'students/professionals/elderly', pain points like 'hard to find things', solutions like 'AI recommendations'), criteria are named but not actually applied, and the stated goal is never referenced again. Insight: content is product- and company-specific (would need significant rework for a different company - Aced's test), choices are argued with trade-offs, at least one idea or prioritisation call is non-obvious yet defended, and earlier decisions are visibly reused later. Grader test: (1) substitution test - replace the product name with a competitor; if the answer still works, cap User/Pain/Solution at 2; (2) linkage test - does the chosen solution trace to the chosen pain point and segment, and the metric to the goal? (3) reasoning test - is there a 'because' after each choice? Structure alone should earn at most 2 on content dimensions and at most 3 on communication.

process_signals.clarifying_questions: 1-3 targeted questions on scope, platform, goal or constraints (e.g. 'Is this for Swiggy's core app or Instamart? Any goal - growth or retention?'). Zero questions is a minor deduction unless assumptions are stated; 6+ questions or questions asking the interviewer to make decisions is a deduction. If candidate states assumptions instead, credit equally.
process_signals.check_ins: Brief check-ins at segment choice, pain point choice and solution choice are positive; asking 'what should I do next?' is negative (Erez).
process_signals.use_of_interviewer_data: If the interviewer supplies a constraint or redirect, strong candidates incorporate it immediately and explain impact; ignoring or resisting redirects is a red flag (Meta accounts). Do not credit the candidate for content the interviewer supplied.
process_signals.pushback_and_hints: Defending a choice with reasons, or changing it with explicit reasoning, both positive. Hint penalty: one light nudge (e.g. 'what about other users?') -> -0.5 on that dimension; a substantive hint that supplies the missing step -> that dimension capped at 2; repeated hand-holding (3+ substantive hints) -> overall capped at Lean No Hire (corpwaters: needing hand-holding is a red flag). [penalty sizes inferred]
process_signals.followups: Meta-style end-of-round conflicting-metric or trade-off probes are part of the score (Aced); grade them under Trade-offs and Metrics.

time_allocation: For ~35 min of case time (Erez): clarify + game plan 3-5 min; goal/motivation 3-5; segmentation 8-10; pain points 8-10; solutions + prioritisation 8-10; metrics/wrap-up 2-4 (metrics allotment inferred). For a 25-30 min case (corpwaters) compress proportionally. Penalties: no chosen solution by the end -> gate cap (Lean No Hire); spending >40% of time on segmentation/clarification -> communication <=2; no metrics because of time -> Metrics 1 but no gate.

hire_thresholds.scale_mapping: Per-dimension 1-4 -> weighted average. Strong Hire: weighted >=3.5 and no dimension <3. Hire: >=3.0 and no dimension <2. Lean Hire: 2.5-2.99, or >=3.0 with one dimension at 2 on a core step. Lean No Hire: 2.0-2.49. No Hire: <2.0 or any must-pass gate at No Hire level. [inferred from equal-must-pass rule in Erez and Aced; no published numeric thresholds]
hire_thresholds.company_scales: Meta interviewers rate competencies Below Expectations / Meets / Strong / Exceptional plus an overall Strong Hire / Hire / Leaning No (IGotAnOffer, ex-Meta coach). Google uses Strong No Hire to Strong Hire 4-point style per Aced and candidate reports; hiring committee is not additive. Aced: acing three dimensions and falling flat on two is not a hire.
hire_thresholds.level_differences: Same thresholds, but anchors are read against level expectations: an APM 3 on Trade-offs would be a 2 for Senior PM.
hire_thresholds.india: No published thresholds found for Swiggy/Flipkart/Zomato/PhonePe/Meesho; candidate reports suggest a single weak core round (product sense) is hard to recover from. [uncertain]

company_differences.Google: Product Design + Favourite Product; rewards bold/big-picture ideas over incremental fixes, user empathy for non-obvious needs, competitor-aware critique in the favourite-product variant; AI prototyping increasingly present. (Aced, Nikka 2020 background)
company_differences.Meta: Product Sense: mission alignment ('connect people'), crisp segmentation and justified prioritisation, ends with conflicting-metric/trade-off follow-up; 2025+ 'Product Sense with AI' round adds prototyping. Metrics depth beyond NSM expected. (Aced Meta blog, Erez)
company_differences.Amazon: No standalone product sense round in most loops; design reasoning assessed via customer obsession, working backwards (PR/FAQ) and product challenge rounds; ability to go from vision to tactical detail. [prep-platform]
company_differences.Microsoft: Design questions within loops often include scenario/user-empathy framing and inclusive design; limited recent source evidence found. [uncertain]
company_differences.Uber: Jam session (group or presentation with PM panel) on an Uber-specific problem; collaboration and marketplace (rider/driver) thinking judged live; format reports disagree. [prep-platform]
company_differences.Indian companies: Swiggy: empathy, pain points, scalable design, often segment-specific prompts (first-time user search, order frequency). Flipkart: e-commerce design (search, discovery, group buy) with metrics and trade-off defence; AI product sense rounds probing evals and guardrails reported. Zomato: design often blended with monetisation/strategy. Meesho: Bharat/tier-2/3 simplicity, non-tech-savvy sellers. PhonePe: UPI ecosystem knowledge. Common India bar difference: stronger expectation to tie design to business outcome and unit economics, and to multi-sided ecosystems (restaurants, riders, sellers). [uncertain: aggregator and practitioner sources, no published rubrics]

calibration_exemplars.1: 'Improve Swiggy': candidate immediately lists 5 features (chatbot, dark mode, loyalty points), no goal, no segment, no metrics; asks interviewer which to pick.
calibration_exemplars.2: Recites goal-user-problem-solution: goal 'engagement', segments 'students/professionals/families', picks students because largest, pain points 'too many options, high delivery fee', solutions 'AI recommendations, discounts', metric 'DAU'. Structured but generic; fails substitution test.
calibration_exemplars.3: Sets goal of repeat orders for new users in tier-2 cities tied to Swiggy's growth; segments by order intent (planned meals, impulse snacks, group orders); picks planned meals with criteria; walks a weeknight dinner journey; 4 specific pains; 3 distinct ideas (meal-plan subscription, 'usual order' one-tap, vernacular voice reorder); picks one-tap on impact/effort; notes restaurant capacity trade-off; metric 14-day repeat rate with guardrails on delivery time and cancellations; checks in twice.
calibration_exemplars.4: All of level 3 plus: ecosystem view incl. restaurants and delivery partners, a non-obvious priority call defended on Swiggy-specific assets (existing order history and dense rider network), a moonshot alongside the MVP, explicit 'what would need to be true' for deferred ideas, a counter-metric for cannibalisation, and a crisp answer to an interviewer pushback on cost by revisiting the earlier goal.

coachable_feedback.Goal and product motivation: In the first 3 minutes, state one company-specific goal in a sentence, then name it again each time you make a choice.
coachable_feedback.User segmentation and choice: Segment by behaviour or need, not age; name two criteria aloud before picking the segment.
coachable_feedback.Pain point identification and prioritisa: Walk one concrete user journey step by step and list at least four problems as frustrations, not features, before choosing one.
coachable_feedback.Solution breadth and creativity: Generate three ideas that could fail independently, deliberately including one bold idea that uses the company's unique assets.
coachable_feedback.Prioritisation and trade-offs: Before choosing, say the criteria; after choosing, name one downside and how you would mitigate it.
coachable_feedback.Success metrics: Give exactly one primary metric with its definition tied to your goal, plus one or two guardrails, and say why each guardrail matters.
coachable_feedback.Structure, communication and collaborati: Open with a 20-second game plan and check in at each of the three choice points instead of asking what to do next.

llm_grading_notes: Length bias: long, framework-complete answers can score high on surface coverage; require the substitution and linkage tests before awarding 3+.
Credit attribution: separate interviewer and candidate turns; never credit segments, pain points or metrics the interviewer proposed unless the candidate adds reasoning.
Keyword leniency: words like 'north star', 'guardrail', 'persona', 'RICE' are not evidence by themselves; require the actual metric/criteria content.
Evidence first: make the model quote transcript lines per dimension before scoring; score 1 when no quote can be found.
Score dimensions independently, then apply gates, then compute overall; do not let a strong communication score lift content dimensions (halo).

Small model (8B) mitigation: one dimension per pass or a short checklist per dimension; give the 1-4 anchors verbatim; include the four calibration exemplars as few-shot; force JSON output with quote fields.
India context: do not penalise use of Indian-market references (UPI, COD, tier-2, vernacular) as off-topic; do reward them only when tied to the chosen user.
Time/landing: detect whether a final solution was chosen; LLMs often miss that the candidate never committed.
